pl-l4d15c3-d1e112.summary: Notes that Jerome says the Egyptians and Israelites were punished temporally lest they be punished eternally, but this is not to be understood of all. Jerome: the human race by the Flood, Sodom by fire, the Egyptians by the sea, and the Israelites in the desert were punished temporally lest they be punished eternally, since God will not judge twice; those punished will not be punished later, or Scripture lies.
claims: Jerome seems to say all those temporally punished escape eternal punishment.

pl-l4d15c3-d1e121.summary: Warns the reader to understand this not of all but only of those who repented under the scourges, believing in the God of the Hebrews; such penance, though brief and momentary, God does not reject.
claims: Jerome's statement applies only to those who repented under punishment.

pl-l4d15c3-d1e127.summary: Shows from Jerome that those not corrected by temporal scourges are later punished eternally: discussing a believer beheaded for adultery, he asks whether he will be punished afterward, making the text false, or not, so that adulterers should wish for brief punishment here.

pl-l4d15c3-d1e132.summary: Continues Jerome: God knows the measures of punishments as of all things; the judge's sentence is not anticipated, nor is his power to punish the sinner taken away; great sin is purged by great and long torments. Those punished, like the one who cursed an Israelite and the Sabbath wood-gatherer, are not punished afterward, since a light fault is compensated by present punishment.
claims: Light faults are compensated by present punishment.
Great sins are punished by long torment.

pl-l4d15c3-d1e139.summary: Draws out that Jerome implies grave sins are punished here and eternally when not repented under the scourge, while light sins punished here are compensated by light punishment; this surely happens in the good, and perhaps in the wicked too.
claims: Unrepented grave sins are punished eternally.
Light sins are compensated by temporal punishment.

pl-l4d15c3-d1e145.summary: Concludes that the prophecy they cited does not support those who say pardon is given by penance for one sin to one who retains another.
claims: Nahum's text does not support partial penance.

pl-l4d15c3-d1e148.summary: Notes they cite other authorities too.

pl-l4d15c3-d1e151.summary: Gives their authority from Gregory: the Lord rains on one city and not another, and on part of a city leaving part dry; when one who hates his neighbor corrects other vices, the city is partly rained on and partly dry, since some cut off some vices but persist gravely in others.
claims: Gregory seems to describe partial correction.

pl-l4d15c3-d1e160.summary: Gives another from Ambrose: the first consolation is that God does not forget to have mercy; the second is through punishment, where, even if faith is lacking, punishment satisfies and relieves.

pl-l4d15c3-d1e172.summary: Gives their argument from reason: if one confesses one sin while keeping another silent and completes the satisfaction, when he later confesses the hidden sin, will penance be imposed for both? This seems far from reason and the Church's custom, which does not impose penance twice for the same sin unless repeated; so that satisfaction was worthy and the sin seems blotted out.

pl-l4d15c3-d1e176.summary: Answers that Gregory's 'raining' refers not to pardon of the crime but to abandoning the act of the sin: part of the city is rained on because one ceases from the act and delight of the sin, not because he has pardon. This continence, instilled from the fount of grace, may lead him gradually to penance or lessen his punishment. If referred to pardon, it would contradict the Gospel: if sins already forgiven return for lack of mercy, much more are unforgiven ones reserved for punishment because of fraternal hatred; and one who has not put off old hatred cannot begin new life.
claims: Gregory's text concerns ceasing from sin, not pardon.
Fraternal hatred prevents pardon of other sins.

pl-l4d15c3-d1e188.summary: Interprets Ambrose's 'even if faith is lacking, punishment satisfies' as concerning not the faith by which one believes in God, but consciousness of the offense: faith is lacking when the sin is not known. Since no one understands all his offenses, if one is punished for a sin he does not know, and bears it patiently and humbly, thinking he may have a sin he does not understand, the punishment satisfies and relieves him.
claims: Ambrose's 'faith' here means awareness of sin.
Patiently borne punishment satisfies for unknown sins.

pl-l4d15c3-d1e206.summary: Answers the objection about satisfaction: it was not satisfaction, since he did not bring forth worthy fruits of penance.
claims: Satisfaction while retaining sin is not true satisfaction.

pl-l4d15c3-d1e213.summary: Cites Augustine: the satisfaction of penance is to cut off the causes of sins and give no entrance to their suggestions.
claims: Satisfaction is cutting off the causes of sin.

pl-l4d15c3-d1e222.summary: Quotes Augustine: those who live wickedly and do not correct their lives, yet keep giving alms, flatter themselves in vain on 'give alms and all is clean'; they do not understand how broad this is. There are many kinds of alms: not only feeding the hungry, but forgiving the penitent, correcting by punishment, restraining by discipline, or praying for the sinner's forgiveness, since these show mercy.
claims: Alms do not cleanse those persisting in sin.
Forgiveness and correction are forms of alms.

pl-l4d15c3.summary: Qualifies Jerome's statement that the Flood, Sodom, the Egyptians, and the Israelites in the desert were punished temporally lest they be punished eternally: it applies only to those who repented under the scourge. Jerome himself, on the adulterer beheaded, says light sins are purged by brief punishment and great ones reserved for eternal torment. So the prophecy does not support remission of one sin while another is retained. Lombard then answers further arguments. Gregory's 'one part of the city rained on' refers to abandoning the act of a sin, not to pardon, since unforgiven hatred keeps sins bound. Ambrose's 'punishment satisfies even if faith is lacking' means lack of consciousness of a sin, not lack of faith in God. The satisfaction done for one sin while retaining another was not true satisfaction, since it did not bear worthy fruits; satisfaction is to cut off the causes of sins, and alms by those persisting in crime do not make them clean, as Augustine says, since alms include forgiveness and correction.
claims: Temporal punishment spares eternal punishment only for those who repent.
Light sins are purged by brief punishment; grave unrepented ones are punished eternally.
Gregory's text concerns ceasing from a sin's act, not its pardon.
Ambrose's text concerns unknown sins, not lack of faith.
Satisfaction while retaining another sin is not true satisfaction.
Satisfaction is cutting off the causes of sin.
